purpose:
To appoint a contractor to maintain the
hoarding and scaffolding at the former Beales / Co-op store
Mansfield, being the site of the Mansfield Connect
development
content:
Mansfield Connect - Hoarding
and Scaffolding
 
 
That
the Design Services Commissioning Manager is authorised to award a
contract via a direct award and associated aspects as detailed in
the attached Exempt Appendix 1 noting that a contracts exemption
form has been approved by the relevant Assistant
Director.
 
That
the Legal Services Manager be authorised to finalise and complete
the appropriate legal agreements, warranties and related
contractual documents.
 
 

On conclusion of the current contract for the soft strip,
link bridges and asbestos removal contract, the former Beales /
Co-op store in Mansfield town centre
will revert back to the Council to
maintain.  The site is required to be
actively managed to ensure public safety and in line with corporate
insurance expectations.  This site is
the subject of the planned development of Mansfield
Connect.
 
The site is required to maintain the hoarding around the
perimeter and the scaffolding at key points, notably along the
façade of Queen Street where aspects of the building are
fragile. The current contractor’s sub-contractors are engaged
in the provision and the scope of the support under this report
includes the costs of power and lighting, testing and inspections
and appropriate licensing from Via / the Highways Authority. Design
Services has been appointed by the Regeneration Manager to procure
the contractor, and the Design Services Commissioning Manager has
facilitated this in consultation with the Corporate Assurance
Manager.
 
The value of the contract and successful contractor are set
out in the Exempt Appendix. It is exempt for publication under
Paragraph 3, Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act 1972 as it
contains commercially sensitive information. It is not in the
public interest to release the information as to do so could
jeopardize the procurement and the appointment.
 
Due to the ongoing hire and
retention of the existing temporary works/services being required
urgently, procurement will be undertaken via an approved Contract
Exception in accordance with the Council’s Contract Procedure
Rules, allowing direct award to a suitably accredited
specialist contractor to avoid unacceptable
delay. In particular, the services are
required so urgently as to preclude the invitation of tenders
and that, in practical terms, no
reasonably satisfactory alternative is available without causing
unnecessary cost, disruption, delay and risk to the
Council.
 

The Council is required to
manage the site on the conclusion of the contract and to be
insurance compliant.  Facilities
Management cannot undertake this work and hence there are no other
options available other than the securing of a contractor for this
work.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to award a contract for maintaining hoarding and scaffolding at a site in Mansfield town center.

purpose:
To approve the purchase of three ride on
mowers.
content:
Purchase of Ride on
Mowing Equipment
 
 
1.
That approval be given to purchase, via a framework, of three
Scag Freedom-Z Zero Turn Ride On mowers
for parks and open spaces for £26,319.00 plus VAT from the
selected supplier as detailed within the appendix; and
 
2. The Legal
Services Manager be authorised to
negotiate, finalise and complete all
necessary legal agreements and other documents to give effect to
the above.
 

 
A
procurement process has been carried out with MDC procurement team
to source the required ride on mowing equipment and following this
process a direct award is permitted on the TPPL Grounds Maintenance, Plant & Handheld Tools
Framework. 
 
The three ride on mowers,
inclusive of a two year warranty, are
required to replace three right standers that have been disposed of
due to them being past their expected life cycle.  Replacement is required in line with the expected
replacement programme on parks plant
equipment and are required to maintain
the current grass cutting regime across all parks and open
spaces. 
 
The purchase of these mowers is being funded from the
existing fleet parks maintenance budget.
 

Market testing has been carried
out to identify alternative plant solutions however the selected
Scag Freedom-Z Zero Turn Ride On mowers
have been identified as providing the best value for money and
quality.
 
A like for like replacement was
considered however the above mentioned
mowers offer a superior quality including, operator comfort, higher
productivity and a greater level of safety due to the lower centre
of gravity and roll over protection system.
 
Not to replace the mowers
– this option was rejected as the existing mowers are past
their life cycle.
topline: The Assistant Director - Neighbourhood Services has decided to approve the purchase of three Scag Freedom-Z Zero Turn Ride On mowers for parks and open spaces.

purpose:
Approval of backpay following employee
regrading
content:
Pay
Reparation
 
To
approve backpay to employee 017208 following re-grading
of post reference LM35
 
 

Following a recent regrading exercise for some colleagues
in Neighbourhood Services, a further
employee (017208) came
forward and requested that post LM35 should be re-evaluated in
order to ensure equality in pay. This request was granted and
following a job evaluation process, the post has been lifted from
Grade 2 to Grade 3, this will be reflected via an amendment to the
Establishment.
 
In line with previous regarding processes and as agreed by
Corporate Leadership Team, the employee will receive backpay to
17th December 2025, the date when CLT approved the
regrading process.
 
Details of the payment can be found at Exempt Appendix 1.
The appendix is exempt under paragraph 1 of Schedule 12A of the
Local Government Act 1972 as it contains information relating to an
individual. It is not in the public interest to release the
information as it relates to the individual circumstances of an
employee

The alternative option is to not approve the
backpay; this would be out of line with payments made to other
employees and could result in a grievance being raised.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to approve backpay for employee 017208 following a re-grading of their post.

content:

12A of the Local Government Act 1972 as it contains commercially

process.
 

Lower resolution projector or

competitive.

decision_maker: Assistant Director of Planning (Chief Planning Officer)
purpose:
To procure a suitably qualified and
experienced project management consultant (Keith Keeley) through
the direct award route to support the development of Mansfield
District Council’s emerging Local Plan as it reaches the
regulation 19 Publication Consultation Stage during September 2026
and then submission of the plan (regulation 22 stage) by no later
than the end of December 2026.
content:
Project Management Consultancy for Mansfield District Local Plan
Review
 
That
the contract for project management consultancy for the Mansfield
District Local Plan review is awarded to the successful contractor
via a direct award as detailed in the attached exempt appendix,
noting that a contract exemption form has been completed by the
relevant Assistant Director.
The
Legal Services Manager be authorised to negotiate, finalise and
complete all necessary legal agreements and other documents to give
effect to the above
 

The key requirement of the
commission is to provide a Critical Friend Project Manager
to:

·      
Sense check the Mansfield Local Plan review
programme of tasks established to date.

·      
Review the evidence collection tasks in the
Smartsheet software programme for timeliness and critical path /
sequence programming

·      
Identify gaps, risks and additional actions in
respect of tasks and evidence collection for timely delivery of the
plan

·      
Provide a mentoring role based on past and present
experience with other Local Authorities to assist the plan being
found sound

·      
Free up planning policy officers to undertake the
tasks required to complete the timely delivery of the
plan. 
 
The contractor has extensive
experience in regeneration and local plan work for local
authorities and provided a similar role in the preparation of the
now adopted Mansfield Local Plan. The contractor is currently
working on a consultancy basis for a number of other local
authorities seeking to submit their Local Plans by December 2026
giving a wide range of experience and insights.
It
is considered the contractor’s input is required for up to 2
days a week initially, before moving a to a one day a week support
approach as the work progresses.
The
Council is close to finalising preparation of the Regulation 19
stage of plan preparationunder the current
plan making regulations. This version of the Local Plan should be
the Council’s final version before it is submitted to the
Planning Inspectorate (PINS) acting for the Secretary of State
(regulation 22 stage) for an Examination in Public
(EIP).
The government has made clear
that the transitional plan making arrangements under the Levelling
Up & Regeneration Act (LURA) will come to an end on the
31st December 2026. Plans prepared after that date will
need to follow the new plan making procedure. It is anticipated
based on advice from the Planning Advisory Service (PAS) that
it’s possible an approximately 2-year delay could ensue
should the deadline for submission by 31 December 2026 be missed
and the new procedure followed. Such a delay could cause a range of
other evidence collected to date, to go out of date with additional
costs to then update. The Adopted Local Plan 2013 - 2033 will also
continue to lose relevance as it becomes further out of date
resulting in a loss of weight in decision making and consequently
the higher risk of decisions being made on a national policy basis
rather than at the local level.
In order to submit to the
Planning Inspectorate (PINS) the emerging Mansfield Local Plan by
31st December 2026, it is estimated that the regulation
19 plan needs to be in draft form by mid-July and published by
18th August in order to go through the appropriate
committee processes for consideration by Overview & Scrutiny,
Portfolio Holder and then by Full Council by the 15th
September 2026 for consultation commencement on the week commencing
21st September 2026. It is proposed subsequent
submission of the plan is by the week commencing 21st
December 2026.
It is considered that in order
to meet this challenging timescale and to prepare a local plan that
is considered sound at the Examination in Public (EIP), good
project management and critical friend assessment is essential for
delivery.
Part of the reasoning is that a
wide range of tasks and evidence collection is coming together at
approximately the same time to inform the plan. The freeing up of
planning policy officers to deliver the necessary local plan
content by drafting and refining the local plan polices and
strategy based on the various studies is therefore now at a
critical stage.
It is considered by appointing
the contractor to the role, the planning policy officers will be
able to the complete the content of the plan to the timetable
indicated in a sound as way as possible for Examination.
Having regard to the above
timelines, a direct award approach is considered necessary in order
for the work to be done in time and for the contractor’s
input to be meaningful in terms of achieving delivery.

i)              
For an officer (s) to undertake the work. However,
it has been identified through project management programming and a
review of risks in delivering the plan to timetable that there
would be a very significant risk of officers being diverted off
their other plan preparation tasks by this work and then failing to
deliver the plan within the prescribed regulatory deadline and
government deadline under the ‘legacy’ transitional
plan making arrangements.
 
ii)            
Not to do the
necessary project management or receive critical friend assessment
in respect of delivery. It is considered that the risk would be
high of project failure in terms of delivery with this approach.
With so many tasks and evidential areas to pull together in a short
period of time, matters such as critical path analysis and sense
checking of realistic delivery times for tasks needed sequentially
will be critical to successful delivery. 
 
iii)          
To do further soft
market testing with other companies able to offer project
management services. Consideration has been given to this option
but the capability of other businesses to be able to do this
specific task at the time required is not known and so would
potentially require soft market testing via a framework approach or
by officers undertaking detailed research with companies in the
wider planning and or project management field. This work would
lead to potentially significant delays in commencement of the work
with the risk of no better outcome than the position established to
date. This is particularly the case given that the contractor was
used by the Council some 11 years ago when a plan was prepared
successfully and it is known the contractor has a respected track
record with the work done with a number of other authorities
preparing their Local Plans.
iv)           
For an officer (s) to undertake the work. However,
it has been identified through project management programming and a

would be a very significant risk of officers being diverted off
their other plan preparation tasks by this work and then failing to
deliver the plan within the prescribed regulatory deadline and
government deadline under the ‘legacy’ transitional
plan making arrangements.
 
v)            
Not to do the
necessary project management or receive critical friend assessment
in respect of delivery. It is considered that the risk would be
high of project failure in terms of delivery with this approach.
With so many tasks and evidential areas to pull together in a short
period of time, matters such as critical path analysis and sense
checking of realistic delivery times for tasks needed sequentially
will be critical to successful delivery. 
 
vi)          
To do further soft
market testing with other companies able to offer project
management services. Consideration has been given to this option
but the capability of other businesses to be able to do this
specific task at the time required is not known and so would
potentially require soft market testing via a framework approach or
by officers undertaking detailed research with companies in the
wider planning and or project management field. This work would
lead to potentially significant delays in commencement of the work
with the risk of no better outcome than the position established to
date. This is particularly the case given that the contractor was
used by the Council some 11 years ago when a plan was prepared
successfully and it is known the contractor has a respected track
record with the work done with a number of other authorities
preparing their Local Plans.

decision_maker: Chief Executive Officer - Key Delegated Decisions
purpose:
To request authority for Officers to enter
into the necessary agreements with delivery partners and grant
recipients, to ensure effective delivery of funded projects within
required timescales.
content:
Record of Decision
Resolved
by the Chief Executive Officer
 
i)   That the projects to be delivered under the
Pride in Place Impact Fund including their respective allocations,
as set out in Appendix 1, be approved subject in each case to an
acceptable grant funding agreement being completed.
 
ii)   That authority be granted to enter into an
agreement with Mansfield CVS for the delivery and management of a
Community Grant Fund (subject to consultation with Programme
Delivery Board), with an allocation of up to £100,000 from
the Pride in Place Impact Fund.
 
iii)   To retain a residual budget of
£116,000 for further applications to be considered
 
iv)   That the Legal Services Manager be
authorised to negotiate, finalise and     complete all necessary
agreements and documentation required to give effect to the
above.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
The recommendations are needed to
ensure that the timely investment of PiP-IF resources is made into the most appropriate
projects, utilising the most effective delivery methods within the
restricted timeframes, while achieving the outputs and outcomes
required by MHCLG
 

 
Do not accept the recommendations
of this report. Failure to approve the proposed approach would
limit the Council's ability to progress funding agreements and
project delivery within the required timescales. Given the limited
delivery period available, this could delay the allocation and
commitment of funding, increase the risk of projects not being
delivered, and potentially result in funding remaining unspent at
the end of the programme. Any unspent funding may be subject to
clawback by MHCLG. In addition, delays to programme delivery could
adversely affect stakeholder confidence and the Council's
reputation as an effective delivery partner.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to approve projects under the Pride in Place Impact Fund and enter into agreements for a Community Grant Fund, aiming for timely investment and effective delivery methods.

purpose:
Appoint a supplier for the crematorium and
cemeteries software
content:
Appointment of Supplier -
Crematorium and Cemeteries Software Replacement
 
 

1.    
To award a 2-year contract with an option to extend
the contract for an additional year via direct award using the
G-Cloud 14 framework to supply the Crematorium and Cemeteries
software, to replace the existing system.  
 

2.     
The Legal Services Manager be authorised to
negotiate, finalise and complete all necessary legal agreements and
other documents to give effect to the above.
 
 

 
The existing crematorium software (BACAS) was
implemented around 25 years ago and while the system was never
fully utilised to its full potential, it currently does not fair
well with more intelligent alternative options.  The current system does not integrate well with
Civica or Govmail systems and does not meet the requirements of the
crematorium’s digitalised service, without the need for
significant investment to the existing software.
 
The current system is not cloud-based and
therefore updates and ‘fixes’ to errors within the
system can become complex and issues cannot be resolved
quickly.
 
An upgrade to the existing system is to provide
further manpower efficiency savings and streamline existing
processes, including online service bookings, cemetery mapping,
memorial ordering, stonemason portal, genealogy searches and
financial management.  Key system
requirements include:
 

·      
Effective
communication with the existing internal finance system to provide
accurate accounting for the bereavement services provision;
reducing the need for staff to work between two systems and
minimising inaccuracies in the data

·      
Provide the
ability for funeral directors to book their own services online,
reducing the time needed for administrative staff to man the
crematorium phones; calls from funeral directors placing bookings,
currently accounts for 75% of all incoming calls

·      
Provide a
facility to be able to map cemetery memorials and log results from
inspection surveys

·      
Provide
cemetery mapping software that allow for members of the public to
access cemetery information online, again reducing manpower
requirements. Grave mapping is a statutory requirement and
currently paper-based cemetery maps are utilised creating
bottlenecks in processing of grave interments and errors from not
having accurate grave information in real time.
 
The current system is administration-heavy
reducing the time spent with families, the vision for the
crematorium is to enhance the service user experience through the
delivery of bereavement support services. Reducing administrative
time will enable officers to engage more in much needed time
supporting families on their bereavement journey with access to
support services and identifying appropriate
memorialisation. 
 
While the service has made steps in digitalising
the process, further improvements can be made with the
implementation of a more intelligent system.
 
The proposed system requires implementation costs
and ongoing annual support costs, and this would incorporate the
fundamental software, mapping software and memorial testing along
with the integration to our existing finance system,
Civica.
 
Through the NCC procurement team, market testing
has been carried out, and this has identified a suitable provider
that delivers an enhanced service, not seen with alternative
providers.  Due to the enhancements with
the system, direct award is appropriate and approved on the
G-Cloud 14 framework.  The required procurement notice has been issued to
NCC procurement team.
 
A data protection
impact assessment has been completed in order to identify and
understand the mitigations required to reduce at data protection
risk.
 
The financing of the replacement software is to be
split between the Joint Crematorium Committee (JCC) and Mansfield
District Council.  The JCC approved the
crematorium element at the committee meeting on the 23rd
February 2026 and the cemeteries element was approved by MDC
Transformation Group.
 

Remain with existing provider - Remaining with the existing provider represents a
mid-range financial option over 3 years. However, the upgrade only
enables cloud hosting and does not significantly improve system
functionality or resolve current operational issues. Annual support
costs remain high, and there are no forecasted efficiency savings
or reductions in administrative workload.
 
Upgrade to alternative systems in
the market – market testing has been
carried out on alternative systems. While alternative providers
provided an enhanced experience, additional mapping costs
significantly increased costs on the basis that an external
provider would have to be sought to carry out this
exercise.  In addition to this, the
additional add-ons to the system provided a far superior
stakeholder experience.
topline: The Director of Corporate Resources/Deputy CEO has decided to appoint a supplier for the replacement of crematorium and cemeteries software.

purpose:
To formally restructure the Housing Repairs
apprenticeship establishment by removing two (2) Property
Maintenance Operations (PMO) apprentice posts (HC65Z) and
establishing one (1) Gas/Plumbing and one (1) Electrical
apprenticeship post in their place.
content:
To
formally restructure the Housing Repairs apprenticeship
establishment by removing two (2) Property Maintenance Operations
(PMO) apprentice posts (HC65Z) and establishing one (1)
Gas/Plumbing and one (1) Electrical apprenticeship post in their
place.
 





The decision is driven by a critical
need to address both national and local skills shortages within
specialised trades:
·      
National
Context:
o  
Electrical Sector: The UK
faces a 5.5% decline in apprenticeship starts despite an estimated
requirement for 12,000 additional electricians by
2030. Currently, fewer than 20% of classroom learners transition into
apprenticeships within a year.
o  
Plumbing Sector:
Approximately 73,700 new plumbers are required by 2032, compounded
by a 47% national dropout rate in construction
apprenticeships.
o  
Long-term Demand: The UK
Trade Skills Index 2024 indicates an urgent requirement for 1.3
million new skilled workers over the next decade.
·      
Local Service Resilience:
o  
A recent review of the
Housing Repairs service identified an ageing workforce and
increasing difficulties in external recruitment.
o  
The service currently
utilises a 27-month PMO program. Transitioning to specialised 36-month
(Plumbing/Gas) and 48-month (Electrical) programs supports a
‘Grow Your Own’ model.
o  
This realignment ensures a
sustainable pipeline of talent to fill future vacancies in
high-demand technical roles, strengthening service
resilience.
Financial Implications
·      
Funding Source: All salary costs will be met through
the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) 2160.
·      
Training Costs: Apprenticeship training fees will be
covered via the Apprenticeship Levy.
·      
Establishment Details:
o  
Working Week: 37 hours
(Monday–Friday).
o  
Duration: 48 months (Electrical) and 36 months
(Plumbing/Gas), including End Point Assessments.

Maintain Status Quo:
Continuing with the current PMO apprentice structure was
considered. However, this was rejected as it fails to address the
specific technical skill gaps in electrical and plumbing teams and
ignores the strategic shift toward higher-level technical
apprenticeships.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to restructure the Housing Repairs apprenticeship establishment to address national and local skills shortages within specialised trades.

purpose:
To enter into contract to deliver Multiverse
delivered digital, data and AI apprenticeship programme as part of
a Nottinghamshire Digital Academy. Multiverse apprenticeships will
support workforce capability in digital, data and AI skills. This
aligns with existing priorities around productivity, service
efficiency, digital transformation and preparation for future
operating models.
content:
1. To enter into a framework
contract to deliver digital, data and AI apprenticeship programme
as part of a Nottinghamshire Digital Academy in the sum of £133,505.20 with
Multiverse; and
 
2.
The Legal Services Manager be authorised to
negotiate, finalise and complete all necessary legal agreements and
other documents to give effect to the above.
 





 
Digital apprenticeships will support workforce capability in
digital, data and AI skills. This aligns with existing priorities
around productivity, service efficiency, digital transformation and
preparation for future operating models. 
The programmes under
consideration are designed for existing staff (a cohort of up to 10
people) and focus on applied learning that delivers tangible
improvements to business processes, data use and decision?making.
Funding is available via the Apprenticeship Levy.
Apprenticeships are delivered
via a tech-driven education provider specialising in apprenticeship
training in data, AI and digital skills. The provider works with
public sector partners to close data skills gaps through
apprenticeships which can be funded through the apprenticeship
levy. If progressed, the apprenticeships would:
 

(a)       
Build practical digital, data and AI
capability;

(b)      
Reduce reliance on a small specialist team for
reporting, automation and analysis;

(c)       
Release staff time through more efficient processes;
and

(d)       
Create a more confident, digitally enabled,
LGR-ready workforce.
 
Success would be measured
through tangible outputs (e.g. improved dashboards, automated
processes, service improvements) alongside qualitative improvements
in capability and confidence.
A
number of other local authorities including Ashfield, Bassetlaw and
Newark and Sherwood have already progressed arrangements with the
apprenticeship provider on a corporate scale or with focussed
cohorts. The council will be working with the proposed provider and
these other councils as part of a joint learning programme
‘Notts Digital Academy’. 
The ‘Notts Digital Academy’ is a unique way of
providing a collaborative approach to deliver an Apprenticeship
Programme that meets the needs of each council.

purpose:
To ensure compliance during the absence of the
Fleet Manager
content:
To
pay an Honorarium for undertaking additional duties to Employee
015237 undertaking Post ETW15 for a period of three months from 1
June 2026, with an option to expend for a further three months if
required.
 

The incumbent of post DTW17 is not able
to attend work for a number of
weeks, the exact timescale cannot be evaluated at this time.
Backfilling arrangements via an agency are being arranged, however
the candidate will not have the full skillset of the postholder and
will be unfamiliar with systems and processes relating to
MDC.
 
In order to ensure compliance in this heavily
legislated area, it is proposed that Employee 015237 undertakes additional duties for a
period of three months to support the induction of the agency
backfill candidate. This employee has a vast knowledge of systems
and processes within this work area and has indicated her
willingness to support the service through this challenging
period.
 
The MDC Honorarium Policy
states that ifcarrying out some duties of
a higher graded post, an honorarium payment will be based on a
percentage of activities. In these circumstances, the honorarium
payment would normally be based on the Officers current spinal
point and the bottom spinal point of the higher graded post with
the appropriate percentage applied (pro rata for part time
employees). It is proposed that employee 015237 will undertake 10%
of the duties of post DTW17, hence the honorarium in this case will
amount to £4,509 per annum or £375.75 per
month.
 
This arrangement will be in place for a period of three
months from the first date of absence of the absent postholder
(28/05/2026), at that point the arrangement will be reviewed. This
ODR contains an option to extend the honorarium for a further

decision_maker: Assistant Director of Planning (Chief Planning Officer)
purpose:
To commission the transport consultants
preparing the local plan to support in Duty to Cooperate
discussions
content:
That the contract for transport
planning and engagement support set out below in connection with
the Mansfield District Local Plan Review is awarded via direct
award to Systra at a cost of
£45,000 noting that the relevant Corporate Director has
approved an exemption form on the grounds of urgency.
 
The Legal Services Manager be
authorised to negotiate, finalise and complete all necessary legal
agreements and other documents to give effect to the
above

 
Mansfield District Council is
currently preparing its Publication Draft Local Plan (in accordance
with Regulation 19 of the Town and Country Planning (Local
Planning) (England) Regulations 2012). The contractor is currently
preparing the transport evidence to underpin the Council’s
Local Plan, including strategic and local transport modelling, to
inform the development, testing and assessment of spatial growth
options.
 
The Council is close to
finalising preparation of the Regulation 19 stage of plan
preparationunder the current plan making
regulations. This version of the Local Plan should be the
Council’s final version before it is submitted to the
Planning Inspectorate (PINS) acting for the Secretary of State
(regulation 22 stage) for an Examination in Public
(EIP).
 
Officers have identified that
transport policies and the supporting evidence for them and
provision of employment and housing growth are likely to be one of
the most important considerations by the Planning Inspectorate
(PINS) in order to establish if the plan is considered sound. To
ensure the risk of being found unsound on Transport matters are
minimised it is considered that the contractor needs to provide
additional support urgently, most particularly in respect of
undertaking:
 

A pre-examination
review of the Local Plan’s transport policy
wording;
To provide support in
preparing Statements of Common Ground (SoCG) in relation to transport, particularly in
relation to National Highways who are responsible for the Strategic
Road Network (SRN) including the M1 which is in close proximity to
MDC and the evidence to date is indicating housing growth will
impact; and in relation to Nottinghamshire County Council Highway
Authority who manage the non SRN in
Nottinghamshire. 
To provide support in
preparing the Local Plan’s Transport Topic Paper;
and
To provide support in
quantifying the highway flows associated with specific development
sites on proposed junction improvements (identified as part of the
mitigation package in the emerging evidence to date)

 
The importance of the above
work and the need for it to be progressed urgently has been
reinforced by feedback from Intelligent Plans (a critical friend
company consisting of very experienced past Local Plan Planning
Inspectors) which has recently reviewed the Transport Issues
flagged by the initial evidence base traffic modelling work by
SYSTRA and correspondence with key stakeholders National Highways
and NCC Highways for MDC.
 
It should be noted the
government has made clear that the transitional plan making arrangements under the Levelling Up &
Regeneration Act (LURA) will come to an end on the 31st December 2026. Plans prepared after
that date will need to follow the new plan making procedure. It is
anticipated based on advice from the Planning Advisory Service
(PAS) that its possible an approximately 2
year delay could ensue should the deadline for submission by
31 December 2026 be missed and the new procedure followed. Such a
delay could cause a range of other evidence collected to date, to
go out of date with additional costs to then update. The Adopted
Local Plan 2013 - 2033 will also continue to lose relevance as it
becomes further out of date resulting in a loss of weight in
decision making and consequently the higher risk of decisions being
made on a national policy basis rather than at the local
level.
 
In order to submit to the
Planning Inspectorate (PINS) the emerging Mansfield Local Plan by
31st December 2026, it is estimated that the regulation
19 plan needs to be in draft form by mid-July and published by
18th August in order to go through the appropriate
committee processes for consideration by Overview & Scrutiny,
Portfolio Holder and then by Full Council by the 15th September 2026 for consultation
commencement on the week commencing 21st September 2026.
It is proposed subsequent submission of the plan is by the week
commencing 21st December 2026.
 
It is considered that in order
to meet this challenging timescale and to prepare a local plan that
is considered sound at the Examination in Public (EIP) a direct
award approach is considered necessary in order for the work to be
done in time.
 

 For
an officer (s) to undertake the work. However, it has been
identified through project management programming and a review of
risks in delivering the plan to timetable and having regard to the
necessary experience required to address key transport issues with
the Highway authority and National Highways that there would be a
very significant risk of officers being diverted off their other
plan preparation tasks by this work and that the officers would not
have the necessary inhouse expertise to withstand the scrutiny that
an Examination would bring without the additional expert
support.
 
 Not to do the additional work.
It is clear from ongoing dialogue with the consultants, NCC
Highways, National Highways, and having regard to feedback from
Intelligent Plans Critical Friend feedback, that the additional
work is required to avoid the likelihood of ‘in principle
objections’ to the plan from National Highways and NCC
Highways and the risk of the Local Plan Review being found unsound
being high. 
 
To do further soft market testing with other companies able
to offer a similar service. However, the contractor has already
been chosen through a robust procurement process in 2024 to lead on
gathering the transport evidence to date, most particularly in
relation to traffic modelling. Going through a further procurement
process for the new tasks set out above would delay the plan so
that the necessary timescales could not be met. Given the
contractor’s involvement to date it is unclear whether there
would be any benefit from engaging in an alternative provider who
would need to get up to speed. Furthermore, at such a late stage in
the Local Plan preparation process and with the tight timescales in
place it is considered unlikely based on officers’ past
experience that alternative providers would be willing to bid or
have the capacity to do the work given no doubt their other work
demands from other local authorities looking to also submit their
plans before 31st December 2026.
topline: The Assistant Director of Planning has decided to award a contract to Systra for transport planning and engagement support for the Mansfield District Local Plan Review to meet the tight deadline before the end of transitional plan making arrangements.

purpose:
1.1 This report summarises the transactions
undertaken during the 2025/26 financial year as part of the
Treasury Management function.
content:
The Financial Services Manager
informed the Committee that the report summarised the transactions
undertaken during the 2025/2026 financial year as part of the
Treasury Management function.
 
The Financial Services Manager
referred the Committee to section 3 of the report, which detailed
the background.  Members of the
Committee were advised that the Treasury Management Strategy had
been underpinned by the adoption of the Chartered Institute of
Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA) Code of Practice on Treasury
Management (the Code) and the CIPFA Prudential Code for Capital
Finance in Local Authorities (the Prudential Code) which includes
the requirements determining a treasury strategy on the likely
financing and investment activity for the forthcoming
year.
 
The Committee was reminded that
the on 4 March 2025 the Council had approved the Annual Treasury
Management Strategy which sets out the Treasury Management
practices adopted by the Council.  That
this report was the final in the series of quarterly reports
prepared and is the final report for the whole of the financial
year.
 
The Committee were referred to
Section 4 and 5 of the report that set out the strategy for
2025/2026.  The Committee was informed
that these sections were provided by the Councils Treasury
Management Advisors called MUFG.  This
provides the background of global economics have an impact on
investments and borrowing.
 
The Members were informed that
section 6 discusses borrowing that has taken place within the
year.  As per section 6.1 during the
period 2025/2026 the Council took out £39M in
borrowing.  As of 31 March 2026, the
Councils total borrowing was just over £85M.  The Committee was informed that most of the debt
had been taken at the Public Works Loans Board as they offer
preferential interest rates to local authorities.  The new borrowing that has been taken out has been
for shorter terms that would have previously borrowed at this is
due to advice by the Council Treasury Management Advisors
MUFG. 
 
Members were informed that
section 7 discusses the investments for the year, and at 7.2 it
shows on 31 March 2026 the Council had £14.5M invested in
financial institutions.  Most of this
investment is held with other local authorities.
 
The Committee was informed that
section 8 provided details of the Councils rate of
return.  The Council had received an
average rate of return of 4.32% against a base rate of 4.02% for
2025/2026.  The Committee was informed
that this rate was due to the Bank of England Monetary Committee
reducing the bank rate from 4.5% to 3.75% between April and
December, which affects the rates the Council can
obtain.  Members were informed that the
Budget was 535K and actual investment achievement received was
£833K this was due to higher interest rates to when the
budget was set.
Andrea Smith Independent Member
had a query related to table 6.5 and asked for if the data
suggested that within the last period there were 7 new long-term
loans taken out within the period.
 
The Financial Services Manager
advised that the year was started with 3 loans of less than 1 year,
then went up to 7 and now we have 10 and that is because we are now
getting advice from the Council Treasury Management Consultant that
you get better rates of return for shorter term loans at the
minute.  So that is why there are more
loans now that are coming in for less than 1 year.
 
The Independent Member asked
for further clarification as to if that was the age of the loan or
is that a 1-year loan.  As the data it
was felt showed it is the maturity of a long-term borrowing not all
borrowing.  As at 6.5 the table stated
that the Tables summaries the long-term borrowing so does that
equate to 7 new long-term borrowing in the period.
 
The Financial Services
confirmed that it did.
The Chair informed the
Committee that the recommendations were that the report be noted
and recommended to Council inline with
the CIPFA Code of Practice adopted by the Council.  Councillor Denness proposed the recommendation and
Councillor Cole seconded the motion.
 
On putting the motion to the
vote, it was unanimously approved.
 
Resolved:
That the recommendations were
that the report be noted and recommended to Council in line with
the CIPFA Code of Practice adopted by the Council.

purpose:
The attached document sets out the audit work
that Forvis Mazars, as the Council’s appointed external
auditors, propose to undertake for the audit of financial
statements for the 2025/26 financial year.
content:
The External Auditor presented a summary of
Audit Strategy Memorandum 2025/2026 to the Committee.  The Financial Statement of the Council is due for
publication at the end of this month. 
The Committee was informed that the external auditors had completed
their planning work earlier in the year and the Audit Strategy
Memorandum for 2025/2026 was the result of the planning work.
 
The key points were highlighted for the
Committee.  Members of the Committee
were directed to page 35 of the report and advised that there was a
new Audit Manager.   The Committee
was informed that on page 36 a timetable of the works with the
completion date of September/early October.  There were no anticipated delays.
 
The Committee was informed that significant
risks were identified for the audit, although not the only items
that are audited, these are the areas that particular attention is
paid to.  All other areas of the
accounts are still tested.
 
Members were referred to page 37 of the report
that identified Management Override of Controls the Committee was
informed that this was a mandated audit risk, so this is found in
every external audit plan.  There were
no particular concerns raised at this authority.
 
The other two identified risks were the
Pension defined benefit liability and the valuation of the
authorities’ land and buildings. 
This is because they are the biggest estimates in the
Council’s accounts.  The Members
were informed that there had been no particular changes in these
other than on the Pension because it is the first year of the
triennial revaluation cycle so there is some work to be done by the
Pension Fund Auditor on their behalf. 
They look at the membership data submitted last year as part of the
valuation process to make sure that it has also been completed
accurately.
 
The Members were informed that the next part
of the report set out the materiality levels which was consistent
with last year at around 2.5 million. 
Members were informed if an error were found over 2.5 Million and
the Council decided not to amend the accounts it would mean that
this would affect our Audit Opinion. 
The external auditor advised that it was very unusual to find an
error of the size.
The Performance materiality level was at
£1.76 million that is the level that is set whereby
everything above that level is tested to ensure that there are not
a number of smaller errors.  Members
were also advised that there was a trivial level of £75K and
all errors above £75K would be referred back to the
Committee.  Errors below that level were
not reported unless it was something that needed to be brought to
the attention of the Committee.
 
Specific Materiality related of £5K in
relation to Senior Officer renumeration disclosures within the
accounts as this is an aspect that members of the public are
particularly interested in, we ensure that the disclosures are as
accurate as possible
 
There was no change in the Value for Money
scope this year and the auditors are still required to look at the
mandated criteria, financial sustainability, governance and
improving economy effectiveness, no new risks have been identified
this year to date.  The identified
weaknesses identified last year as per page 45 and 46 will be
followed up.  This was related to bank
reconciliation and Housing repairs as discussed in the meeting
today.
 
Councillor Moxon queried that in general
within the audit market there was a shortage of auditors for the
public sector is this still the case or has this been resolved.
 
The auditor responded that the government were
still looking at the future of local audit and a new body is being
introduced called the Local Audit Office from 2028 which will
manage the audit of Councils and the NHS.  Going back to the Audit Commission
style.  Mazars are sufficiently
resourced and advised that they were still investing in
training.  There were no concerns
locally, however, nationally there was still a skills shortage.
 
The Director Corporate Resources/Deputy CEO
informed the Committee that there was a requirement to publish the
accounts by the end of June 2026 and to advise the Committee that
the accounts for 2025/2026 had been published.  Thanks to the Financial Services Manager and the
team’s hard work.
 
The Chair informed the Committee that the
recommendations were that the External Audit Strategy Memorandum
for 2025/2026 be noted.
 
Councillor Moxon proposed the recommendation,
and this was seconded by Councillor Denness.
 
The motion was confirmed by a show of
hands.
 
Resolved:
That the External Audit Strategy Memorandum
for 2025/2026 be noted.
topline: The Audit, Governance & Standards Committee has decided to approve the External Audit Strategy Memorandum for 2025/2026.

content:
The Corporate Assurance Manager
presented a summary of the report to the Committee.

Members were informed that the report detailed the
results of the self-assessments completed by the Corporate
Assurance Manager of the Council’s counter fraud and
corruption framework and arrangements against recommended good
practice detailed in: Local Government Counter Fraud and Corruption
Strategy for the 2020s – “Fighting Fraud and Corruption
Locally” and the Chartered Institute of Finance and
Accountancy’s (CIPFA) Code of Practice “Managing the
Risk of Fraud and Corruption”

 

The Committee was informed that all Policies and
Procedures are reviewed.  The Committee
was referred to 4.2 of the report to indicate that there had been
an amendment to the Whistleblowing Act, with the addition of
reporting of Sexual Harassment.  This
amendment had been applied in April 2026.

 

The Corporate Assurance Manager informed the
Committee that overall, there were very sound arrangements and the
Council’s Whistleblowing arrangements are highly effective
and there was confidence across the Council that things were taken
seriously and investigate where possible to do so.  These will be assessed to find out the best avenue
for the investigation to take place. This may be referred to
Officers to investigate.

 

If a serious matter this would be dealt with by
Internal Audit.  It was reported that
several investigations had taken place and some were
ongoing.

 

Members were referred to item 14 which advised that
an Annual Reminder would be sent in relation to Declarations of
Interest and Hospitality just to clarify what needs to be declared
and how this is to be done.   
Members were then referred to page 99 and item 31.  Members of the Committee were informed that when
completing the NFI many potential matches are identified
particularly related to Council Tax. 
These are sample checked due to resources.  The Cabinet Office is notified of
this.  The high-risk ones are
prioritised and completed wherever possible to do so.

 

 

The Committee was referred to Table 2 and advised
that overall, the arrangements were sound.

 

The Committee was referred Table 3 the Fraud and
Corruption Register and informed that this was reviewed annually
and advised that the information was in risk rating
order.  The majority are rated low with
the mitigations that are in place. 
However, procurement and contract management which covers both
internal and external fraud and corruption from the contractors
themselves, which include instances of duplicated invoices being
submitted with slight amendments to the wording.  Therefore, this is a high risk

 

A Member queried what would happen if this were
found to be the case and what action would be taken against the
perpetrator.

 

The Corporate Assurance Manager advised that this
could result in a contract being terminated and if fraud were
proven this would be referred to the Police for further
action.

 

Director of Corporate Resources/Deputy CEO informed
the Committee that to prevent issues of fraud further processes and
procedures had been implemented.

 

The Corporate Assurance Manager advised that where
needed some contractors and sub-contractors had been terminated and
had received no further works

 

Andrea Smith (Independent Member) asked if the
Housing Repairs Action Plan fed into mitigating this, although not
expressly referenced it does appear to be very connected, and in
terms of reducing this down to a 6 is that in line with the target
date of 31 July 2026.  So that this can
be reassessed at that time to assess if this is now at a more
tolerable level.

 

The Corporate Assurance Manager agreed that it was
the case that it was linked currently along with the Corporate
Actions that include Contract Management Guidance and
Arrangements.  There is monthly
monitoring of spend with contractors to ensure that there are
appropriate contracts in place and the proper governance
arrangements in place and that the target date of 31 July 2026 was
achievable.  To be able to bring this
level back into the tolerable range.

 

There will be a Procurement Workshop at the
beginning of July with the departments that have been identified as
needing this, to support their training needs and resolve any
issues to compliance.  This will be an
interactive session.  The high rating at
the moment is correct. 

 

The Chair advised that the recommendations were that
the results of the assessments of the Council’s counter fraud
and corruption framework and arrangements detailed in Tables 1
& 2 be noted and that the revised corporate fraud and
corruption risk register enclosed as Table 3 be considered prior to
formal approval by the Assistant Director of Law, Governance and
People.

 

Councillor Cole proposed that the recommendations be
approved, Councillor Hughes seconded this.

 

On putting the motion to the vote, it was
unanimously approved.

 

Resolved:

i)         
That the results of the assessments of the Council’s counter
fraud and corruption framework and arrangements detailed in Tables
1 & 2 be noted

 

ii)         That the
revised corporate fraud and corruption risk register enclosed as
Table 3 be considered prior to formal approval by the Assistant
Director of Law, Governance and People
topline: The Council has approved recommendations regarding their counter fraud and corruption framework and arrangements.

content:
The Assistant Director for
Housing summarised the Housing Repairs and Procurement update
report for the Committee.
 
The Committee was informed that
the report was an update on the Action Plan progress out of actions
from a Housing and Procurement Audit Review.  The Committee was informed that the Audit Team and
Finance had supported the Housing Team with this.
 
The Committee was referred to
the two appendices attached to the report.  The Members were informed that appendix one was a
copy of the Action Plan which was represented at the last
Governance and Standards Meeting and at that meeting Members had

content:
Title/Reference: 
Changes to the Establishment - Review of
Legal Services and addition
of Deputy Statutory Officer Allowances
 
Approval of the following changes to the establishment in Legal
Services as set out in the appendix:
 

a)   
Addition of 1x Full Time Equivalent (FTE) Principal
Lawyer (Grade 7)

b)   
Addition of 1x FTE Lawyer (Career Grade 5/6) or
1xFTE trainee lawyer (Grade 4) dependent on successful recruitment
to the principal posts

c)    
Addition of 1x FTE Legal and Information Governance
Assistant (Grade 2 – subject to Job Evaluation)

d)   
Addition of a Deputy Statutory Officer allowance for
the Deputy Monitoring Officer and the Deputy Section 151 Officer at
£3000 per year.
 
 

 

1.1             
The Legal Services Team offers critical support to
Mansfield District Council, giving professional legal and
governance advice, managing and reviewing legal strategies on
behalf of the Council, preparing legal documents including complex
contracts, instructing external legal support and counsel,
litigation, including advocacy, and reviewing reports and decisions
amongst many other tasks. The service seeks to ensure the council
is protected from legal action, that its own actions are taken
appropriately and that the interest of the council is best served
from a legal perspective.

 

1.2             
The Team has been working under increasing pressure
for some time as a result of:

a)   
A large number of
major cases and council projects requiring
significant legal expertise and input many of which will not be
concluded before Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).

b)   
A significant increase in housing disrepair
litigation cases

c)    
Increase in demand from client departments and
tightening of governance processes.

 

1.3             
In addition, moving forward, significant legal input
will be required on Local Government Reorganisation both directly
within the Legal and Governance workstream, including involvement
in the drafting of the Section 16 agreement, and indirectly via the
provision of legal advice to the other workstreams.

 

1.4             
As well as managing increased demand, the team has
been working under-capacity for some time due to vacancies. The
service has been reliant on locum lawyers to cover these vacancies
and manage demand resulting in a cost to the council of
c.£300k pa. In addition, while the locum support currently
working with the Council has been good and stable, attempts to fill
other vacancies with locum support have been unsuccessful. There
has also been further reduction in legal expertise within the
Council due to the current Assistant Director having a governance
rather than legal professional background.

 

1.5             
The service manager currently manages the major
project work in addition to the routine workload as well as having
direct line management responsibility for every member of the team.
The level of demand on the service is challenging resulting in a
slower than optimum response to requests from client departments,
delays in for example, contractual work, and potential increased
risk to the Council’s interests. It has also resulted in an
increase in the amount of work having to be outsourced (largely to
commercial legal services provided by other local
authorities).

 

1.6             
The proposed structure seeks to consolidate the
locum posts within the establishment, thereby increasing the
capacity of the team to better manage demand and increasing its
resilience. No current members of establishment staff would be at
risk or would experience any changes to their roles, with the exception of line management
arrangements.

 

1.7             
The proposed structure would bolster the tier of
legally qualified management between the Legal Services Manager and
the rest of the team through filling the currently vacant Principal
Lawyer post and introducing a second Principal Lawyer. One
Principal would specialise in Contracts and the other in Housing/
Litigation. They would share line management responsibility for the
remainder of the team, freeing up capacity at the Service Manager
level to focus on major projects and significant legal
matters.

 

1.8             
The vacant lawyer post would be filled and an additional lawyer role would be
introduced, funded via the HRA, to work exclusively on Housing
disrepair litigation (this addition was captured as part of the
2025-26 budget process). This leaves the team with four qualified
lawyers, two Principal Lawyers and the Legal Services
Manager.
 

1.9             
At the Assistant level it is proposed that an
additional full-time assistant is added at Grade 2 to support Right
to Buy applications and Information Governance bringing the total
Assistant support to 2.6 FTE (2x FTE, 1x 0.6 FTE). A matrix
management arrangement would be put in place between Legal and
Information Governance Services to manage the new Assistant post
with their time being split between the services on a 60% Legal
Services, 40% Information Governance Services basis.
 

1.10          
Deputy Statutory Officer Allowances

The Council is required to appoint a Monitoring
Officer and a Section 151 Officer who have individual statutory
responsibilities in relation to the legal and financial operation
of the Council. Deputies are appointed to act in the absence of the
Statutory Officers and to support the statutory officers in
carrying out their duties. The Legal Services Manager is currently
appointed as Deputy Monitoring Officer
and the Financial Services Manager is currently appointed as the
Deputy Section 151 Officer.

 

1.11          
Currently both roles only specify acting in the
absence of the Statutory Officer but with increasing demands on
both statutory roles, including those related to LGR it is likely
that there will be an increase in the levels of support with
statutory officer responsibilities beyond acting in the absence of
the relevant statutory officer. In addition, in relation to the
Deputy Monitoring Officer, as the current Monitoring Officer is not
legally qualified, there is an increased reliance on the Legal
Services Manager for support with the legal aspects of the
Monitoring Officer role.

 

1.12          
To reflect these changes
it is proposed that an additional £3000 pa Deputy Statutory
Officer allowance is paid to the postholders designated as Deputy
MO and Deputy Section 151 Officer. This is common practice in many
other authorities and the level of the allowance proposed is the
average of a number of district
authorities across the country, including in
Nottinghamshire.
 
 

To continue to use locum and external support to meet demand.
This option was rejected as it would see the increased costs
continue and would not relieve the pressure on the team.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to approve recommendations for changes to the establishment in Legal Services, including adding new staff positions and introducing Deputy Statutory Officer allowances.

content:
OneAdvanced Dynamic Resource
Scheduling (DRS) software
 
 
1.
To approve the renewal of our open-ended contract with OneAdvanced
for the provision of the Dynamic Resourcing Schedule (DRS) via a
direct award through the Crown Commercial Services (CCS) Framework
for a period of three years and at the cost outlined in the report
below; and
 
2.
To approve the one-off cost of £6,505
for upgrading the current version of the DRS; and
 
3.
If required, the Legal Services Manager be authorised to negotiate,
finalise and complete all necessary legal agreements and other
documents to give effect to the above.
 

The renewal of the DRS ensures
continuity of our Repairs service, maintains regulatory compliance,
minimizes operational risk, and delivers value for money through a
compliant procurement route.
 
One of the most critical
elements of the Council’s Repairs service is the effective
planning and scheduling of jobs, currently managed through the DRS
system provided by OneAdvanced. This system underpins day-to-day
operational delivery, ensuring repairs are planned efficiently,
resources are allocated appropriately, and service standards are
met for customers.
 
The current version of DRS is
outdated and no longer fully supported. Continuing to rely on an
unsupported system poses growing operational, security, and
service-delivery risks, including system failure, reduced
functionality, and an inability to respond to future service
requirements or regulatory changes.
 
Upgrading to the latest
supported version of DRS will improve system reliability and
provide access to enhanced functionality and ongoing vendor
support. This investment will reduce risks to service delivery, and
enable the repairs service to operate more efficiently and
sustainably in future.
 
The current contract is an
open-ended contract, renewing annually on 26 October 2026 and
whilst an open-ended IT contract is not automatically unlawful, it
could breach the Procurement Act 2023, especially around
transparency, modification, and fair competition.
 
The renewal of our open-ended contract with OneAdvanced via
a direct award through the Crown Commercial Services (CCS)
Framework for a period of three years will
ensure continuity of a critical operational service service,
maintain regulatory compliance and deliver value for money through
a compliant procurement route.
 
The exemption has been approved in advance of this
decision
The period of the contract has been proposed taking into
consideration the potential implications and impact on our current
business operations, IT infrastructure and Local Government
Re-organisation.
 
The Council’s Procurement
Unit were consulted throughout the process as well as the
Council’s Transformation Group. 
The 36-month contract with OneAdvanced includes a total cost of
£48,143 along with a One-Off cost for upgrading the current
version of £6,505
 

Whilst undertaking a full
market tender will fully test the competitiveness of the market,
due to the lengthy process required for this option and the short
timescale before the existing contract expires, the option to
undertake a full market tender is not an option at this
stage.
 
Potential costs of switching to
an alternative supplier and the transition and implementation time
ranges of a new system the potential disruption to service during
this period coupled with the need to continually deliver against
the consumer standards whilst under close scrutiny by the Social
Housing Regulator would pose a significant risk and is therefore
not an option at this stage.
topline: The Assistant Director - Housing has decided to renew the contract with OneAdvanced for the provision of the Dynamic Resourcing Schedule (DRS) software for a period of three years.

purpose:
Approval of the annual CAMEO mercury abatement
burden sharing fees
content:
Approval of CAMEO abatement
fees
 
Delegated Decision Ref:
26/11/NS
 
This
report seeks approval for the payment of the annual Mercury
Abatement CAMEO fee of £55,696
 

Payment is required to offset
the impact of the Crematoriums non-abated  
cremations annually as required
by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
(DEFRA).
 
In 2005
Defra introduced a requirement for the cremation industry to
remove
mercury
from 50% of cremations. The national target, based on the
available
science,
achieves a proportionate response for removing mercury
from
cremations, whilst not burdening the bereaved with excessive
cost and the
possibility of closing of local crematoria.
 
Along with
the 50% target the principle of “burden sharing” was
introduced, a
process
whereby Operators who could install abatement plant do so, and the
cost
is shared
with those could not install such abatement equipment. Defra
recognised
this as
the most equitable way of achieving the target, whilst the cost or
“burden” is
shared by
the entire sector.
 
The
cremators installed within Mansfield Crematorium currently do not
have
abatement
equipment installed and therefore a fee is payable for 50% of
the
cremations
carried out annually.
 
The fee
for 2025 is £59 per cremation and Mansfield Crematorium
carried out
1887
cremations during this year.  The charge
is only payable on 944 of these
cremations
given that only 50% is required to be abated.
 

 
There is no alternative option
to payment of the fees as we have a responsibility to do so under
the Environmental Act 1990.
topline: The Assistant Director - Neighbourhood Services has decided to approve the payment of an annual Mercury Abatement CAMEO fee for cremations at Mansfield Crematorium.

decision_maker: Assistant Director of Law Governance and People
content:
Renewal of Service Level
Agreement with Nottinghamshire County Council for Delivery of
Procurement Service
 
 
 
To
extend the current service level agreement with Nottinghamshire
County Council for the delivery of a procurement service until
31st March 2028 at an annual cost of
£65,000.
 
 

It is
proposed that the Council extends the current SLA with
Nottinghamshire County Council for the provision of procurement
advice and support. The County Council will undertake procurement
exercises for relevant contracts with an estimated contract value
exceeding £50,000 for non-construction related projects and
£100,000 for construction related projects. Below those
thresholds, the procurement exercise would be undertaken in-house.
This is considered to be the best option for the Council for the
following key reasons
Ø 
The County Council has the experience,
knowledge and resource resilience required to support delivery of
this Council’s future planned procurement projects until
31st March 2028 including a number of major capital
projects
Ø 
The County Council is committed to
working with this Council to maximise the delivery of social value
outcomes which is a key element of this Council’s current
Procurement Strategy whilst still aiming to deliver significant
savings
Ø 
The County Council meets this
Council’s aim of using local service providers wherever
possible
Ø 
The County Council is also a local Anchor
Institution with which this Council is committed to work in
collaboration for the benefit of the local community
 
Nottinghamshire County
Council’s annual fee for the service is to be reviewed
annually and can increase in line with salary cost increases and if
additional services are required.
 
The Service Level Agreement
will include a set of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) which are
agreed between both parties to monitor and manage the performance
of the contract. It also includes the social value measures that
will be included in all above threshold procurement
projects.
This is not a relevant
contract for the purposes of the Procurement Act 2023 and the
Council’s Contract Procedure Rules. This is a collaborative
arrangement where the key drivers are to share expertise and costs
between two partner organisations.
The proposal is to extend the
current Service Level Agreement to 31st March 2028 under
the same terms and conditions.

Due to Local Government
Reorganisation, no other viable options are feasible at this
time

purpose:
Remove two vacant joinery posts Housing
Repairs Service (Post Ref HC05B), and add 2 x FTE to the position
of Property Maintenance Operatives, Housing Repairs.
content:
Change of Establishment
from Joinery role to Property Maintenance Operative role
 
Delegated Decision
Ref:  26/13/CEO
 
Remove two vacant joinery posts
Housing Repairs Service (Post Ref HC05B),and add 2 x FTE to the
position of Property Maintenance Operatives, Housing
Repairs

 
1.
Strategic Workforce Planning and National Context
The UK Trade Skills
Index 2024 identifies a critical national shortage of skilled
tradespeople, a deficit projected to persist until at least 2032.
This shortage is particularly acute in traditional crafts such as
plumbing, bricklaying, and carpentry. Internally, a recent review
of the Housing Repairs Service confirms an ageing workforce profile
and increasing difficulty in external recruitment. Transitioning to
a Property Maintenance Operative (PMO) model allows the Council to
adopt a "Grow Your Own" strategy, ensuring a sustainable talent
pipeline and long-term service resilience.
 
2.
Practical Application and Apprenticeship Success
There are currently
four apprentices within the service at various stages of the Level
2 PMO standard. Two apprentices are projected to complete their
qualifications by May–June 2026. Over the past 24 months,
these individuals have gained a diverse competency set including
joinery, bricklaying, tiling, painting / decorating, basic
plumbing, and electrical safety. Creating these permanent roles
onto the establishment ensures these skills and provides a clear
career pathway for the Council’s own trainees.
 
3.
Operational Efficiency and Service Delivery
The shift from
single-trade joinery roles to multi-skilled PMO roles offers a
"cross-platform" approach to repairs. This evolution
facilitates:

First-Time Fix
Rates: One operative can address multiple
minor issues (e.g., repairing a door frame and patching the
associated plasterwork) in a single visit.
Planning
Efficiency: Reduces the logistical burden
of coordinating multiple trades for minor reactive
repairs.
Improved Tenant
Experience: Minimises the number of
appointments required for residents, leading to higher satisfaction
levels.
Greater
Resilience: With the cross-trade skills
that these roles provide, therefore allowing operational support to
teams that are experiencing higher workloads.

 
4.
Enhanced Operational Flexibility and Statutory
Compliance
Increased Capacity
for Void Turnaround

·      
The transition to a PMO model provides significantly
greater flexibility within the Voids Management workflow.
Traditional joinery roles are often limited to specific
timber-based repairs, creating bottlenecks when other minor
trades (tiling, plastering,or
basic plumbing) are required to make a property "re-let ready."
PMOs can execute a wider scope of the "void specification"
independently, reducing the number of different operatives required
per property. This streamlined approach directly contributes to a
reduction in Key-to-Key times, minimising rental income
loss.
Addressing Damp,
Mould, and Awaab’s Law
·      
With the implementation of Awaab’s Law (Social
Housing Regulation Act), the Council is under a strict statutory
obligation to investigate and remediate damp and mould within
specific, mandatory timescales.

Multi-Disciplinary
Response: Damp and mould issues are rarely caused by a single
factor. A PMO possesses the cross-trade skill set required to
address the multi-faceted nature of these repairs — for
example, fixing a minor plumbing leak (plumbing), replacing a
damaged skirting board (joinery), and applying fungicidal
treatments (painting / decorating).
Early Intervention:
Providing a multi-skilled operative at the first point of contact
ensures that "easy fixes" are completed immediately, preventing
minor damp issues from escalating into significant category 1
hazards.
Compliance
Resilience: This flexibility is essential for meeting the rapid
response times mandated by the new legislation, ensuring the
Council remains compliant and avoids the legal and financial
penalties associated with failure to repair.

 
5.
Financial and Job Evaluation Implications
The proposed PMO roles
align with existing salary scales for craft workers. It is
anticipated that the Person Specification (PS) for the PMO will
reflect a composite of joinery and bricklaying competencies,
calibrated at a level that maintains pay parity with current craft
rates. Consequently, this change is cost-neutral to the Housing
Revenue Account (HRA) while providing a more versatile
workforce.
As part of the
department’s succession planning, the PMO role opens further
opportunities for this type of apprenticeship alongside trade
specific needs, where the need is identified.
 
                                                                                                                
 

An alternative option
would be to recruit to the single trade position; however, this is
not recommended as it would provide less resilience within the
service than a Property Maintenance Operative.  As these give a broader range of skills and
knowledge which can be fully utilised across the
service.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to transition vacant joinery posts to Property Maintenance Operative roles to address a national shortage of skilled tradespeople and improve service efficiency.

purpose:
Approval is given to appoint a specialist
structural engineering consultant to act on behalf of Mansfield
District Council in relation to the partial collapse of Walkden
Street Multi-Storey Car Park
content:
Appointment of
consultant/expert witness in relation to the partial collapse of
Walkden Street Car Park in Mansfield
 
Delegated Decision Ref
26/12/CEO
 
Approval is given to appoint a specialist structural engineering
consultant to act on behalf of Mansfield District Council in
relation to the partial collapse of Walkden Street Multi-Storey Car
Park, including provision of expert technical advice and expert
witness services for the purpose of defending the Council’s
positions as leaseholder and building control authority, as
detailed within Exempt Appendix A.
 
The
Design Services Commissioning Manager is authorised to award the
consultancy contract and manage the appointment within the approved
budget provision, with remaining budget retained to address
contingencies and unforeseen requirements arising from the incident
and associated legal action.
 
Authority is delegated to the Legal Services Manager to
negotiate, finalise and complete all necessary contractual
agreements and associated documentation required to give effect to
this decision.
 

A
partial structural collapse has occurred at Walkden Street
Multi-Storey Car Park. The Council has obligations and potential
liabilities arising from the incident, including matters associated
with the terms of its lease and any resultant legal claims or
disputes.
Independent specialist structural engineering expertise is
required to determine the likely cause and mechanism of failure,
advise on structural condition and safety considerations, and
support the Council’s legal position through provision of
expert witness services.
Failure to appoint an appropriately qualified consultant
would expose the Council to significant financial and legal risk
and limit its ability to make informed decisions regarding
demolition, retention, liability and recovery actions.
Three specialist structural engineering consultants with
recognised expert witness capability were invited to provide
quotations for the required services. All consultants were selected
from an established professional register of structural engineering
expert witnesses to ensure appropriate technical competence and
independence.
 

The option of not appointing a
specialist consultant was considered but rejected as this would
leave the Council without independent technical advice or expert
witness support in relation to a significant structural failure,
exposing the Council to substantial legal and financial
risk.
topline: The Chief Executive Officer has decided to appoint a specialist structural engineering consultant to address the partial collapse of Walkden Street Car Park in Mansfield.

Mansfield District Council requires a contractor to carry

Cemetery, and a procurement exercise has been
undertaken. 
 
The chapel is utilised to house burial services within the
cemetery and is the location for the Friends of Mansfield Cemetery
events.  Given the grade two listed
status the necessary conservation advice has been sought and
approved for the work to proceed.

are costly and will increase to the project spend
significantly.  Bat roosting takes place
between April and October and the current ecology license takes
account of the works being carried out prior to bat roosting
season.
